HotFlashReferenceLibrary.intro: General background on what current research says about hot flashes — not specific to your own record, and not medical advice.

hormonal_signaling.heading: Hormonal signaling
hormonal_signaling.body: During the menopause transition, estrogen production declines and its signaling to the brain's temperature-regulation centers changes. This shift is the starting point most current research points to for why hot flashes begin during this stage of life, though the full chain from hormonal change to a hot flash involves several more steps described below.

kndy_nk3_pathway.heading: The KNDy / neurokinin / NK3 pathway
kndy_nk3_pathway.body: As estrogen signaling changes, a group of neurons in the hypothalamus known as KNDy neurons (named for the signaling molecules kisspeptin, neurokinin B, and dynorphin) become more active. Their neurokinin B signaling activates NK3 receptors in the brain's thermoregulatory center, which appears to narrow the body's tolerance for small changes in core temperature — so a change that wouldn't normally register gets interpreted as overheating, and the body responds with the sweating and vasodilation of a hot flash. This pathway is one of the more specific mechanistic models current research has identified, and it's the basis for newer nonhormonal treatments described in the treatment pathways section below.

neurotransmitter_pathways.heading: Serotonin, norepinephrine, and other nonhormonal pathways
neurotransmitter_pathways.body: Separately from the NK3 pathway, medications that affect serotonin, norepinephrine, or GABA — neurotransmitter systems more commonly associated with mood and pain — have also been studied for hot flashes. These systems interact with the same thermoregulatory circuits, which is thought to be why some medications originally developed for other conditions can also affect hot flash frequency or severity for some people.

behavioral_psychological.heading: Behavioral and psychological factors
behavioral_psychological.body: A hot flash is a physiological event, but how disruptive it is depends partly on separate factors — stress, sleep, and how the sensation is interpreted in the moment. Behavioral approaches such as cognitive behavioral therapy and clinical hypnosis have been studied for their effect on this second layer: some research suggests they can reduce how much hot flashes interfere with sleep, concentration, or daily life, and possibly their frequency or severity too, through central and psychological pathways rather than a direct effect on peripheral blood vessels.

context_lifestyle.heading: Context and lifestyle factors
context_lifestyle.body: Caffeine, alcohol, diet, room temperature, and other everyday factors are commonly discussed as hot flash "triggers," but current evidence for a direct, consistent relationship is limited and mixed. This is exactly why EMBR records context like this as an observation — what was reported alongside what — rather than presenting it as a cause. A pattern showing up together on several days is worth noticing; it isn't the same as proof that one caused the other.

treatment_pathways.heading: Treatment pathways clinicians consider
treatment_pathways.body: Several categories of treatment target different points in the pathways above: hormone therapy addresses the underlying hormonal signaling; NK3 receptor antagonists (such as fezolinetant) specifically block the KNDy pathway described above and were approved based on that mechanism; certain nonhormonal medications affect serotonin/norepinephrine/GABA signaling; and behavioral approaches address the psychological and functional layer. Each has a different evidence base, different candidates it's suited to, and different risks — for example, NK3 receptor antagonists carry a monitoring requirement for rare liver effects, and hormone therapy's suitability depends heavily on individual health history.
treatment_pathways.caveat: This describes categories of treatment used in clinical practice, not a recommendation for you. Whether any of these is appropriate depends on your own health history, and that's a conversation for you and your clinician — EMBR doesn't select or recommend treatments.

HotFlashReferenceLibrary.caveat: This section summarizes general scientific and clinical literature on hot flashes. It isn't a diagnosis, an explanation of the cause of your own symptoms, or medical advice.

meta.title: EMBR | Evidence infrastructure for menopause
meta.description: EMBR helps you track symptoms, see patterns over time, and turn your experience into evidence for your healthcare conversations.

hero.headline: Make sense of what you're experiencing.
hero.body: EMBR helps you track symptoms, see patterns over time, and turn your experience into evidence you can bring into your healthcare conversations.
hero.trust: Not a diagnosis. Not medical advice. A clearer record for you and your healthcare conversations.
hero.loopLabel: How EMBR works, in four steps

story.headline: Your symptoms are data.

moments.m3: The afternoon you could not concentrate.

story.body: When those moments are scattered across memory, notes and appointments, the bigger picture is easy to lose.
story.kicker: EMBR helps you capture the pattern.

track.label: Track
track.title: Capture what you're experiencing.
track.body: Log symptoms with severity, cycle entries, daily context like sleep and stress, and the treatments you try. A hot flash can be a single tap.

patterns.label: See patterns
patterns.title: Understand changes across time.
patterns.body: Your timeline and Signals show how often symptoms appear, which ones occur together, and how your cycle has changed.

brief.label: Build your brief
brief.title: Turn your record into a structured summary.
brief.body: Choose a date range and EMBR builds an EMBR BRIEF from what you've logged in it.

care.label: Prepare for care
care.title: Bring clearer evidence into the conversation.
care.body: Review the brief, download it as a PDF, and take it to the conversation with your healthcare provider.

product.headline: From symptom tracking to evidence.
product.body1: An ordinary symptom tracker stores entries. EMBR connects them. Every log becomes part of a dated, longitudinal record, and that record feeds directly into a structured summary built for a healthcare conversation.
product.body2: Patterns come from fixed, transparent rules applied to what you've logged, not from guesswork. When EMBR shows a signal, you can see the days it came from.

record.title: One dated record
record.body: Symptoms, cycle entries, daily context and treatments sit on the same timeline, so nothing has to be pieced together later.

signals.title: Signals with their evidence
signals.body: When two symptoms are logged on the same day at least three times, EMBR shows it, along with the dates behind it.

brief.title: Connected to your brief
brief.body: The same record becomes the summary you bring to your appointment. Nothing re-entered, nothing reconstructed from memory.

brief.headline: A clearer way to walk into the appointment.
brief.body: EMBR turns your tracked symptoms, cycle information, patterns and relevant history into a structured EMBR BRIEF that you can review and bring into a healthcare conversation.
brief.disclaimer: It is a summary of your recorded data, not a diagnosis and not medical advice.

points.contents: Symptom frequency, a cycle summary, the treatments you logged, and how the period compares with the one before.
points.evidence: Each pattern links back to the dates it was logged, so it can be checked rather than taken on trust.
points.questions: Suggested questions for you to raise. Not treatment recommendations.
points.pdf: A PDF you can download, print or share with the person you're seeing.

brief.clinician: Your healthcare provider makes the clinical decisions. EMBR helps you arrive with a clearer record.

evidence.headline: Your experience deserves a record.
evidence.body1: Menopause symptoms rarely arrive all at once. They unfold over weeks and months, shift in intensity, and overlap with sleep, stress and everything else going on.
evidence.body2: That makes them hard to remember accurately and hard to describe in a short appointment. What gets said in the room is often a summary of the last few days, not the last few months.
evidence.body3: A consistent, dated record helps close that gap. Not by interpreting your body for you, but by making sure what you experienced is written down.

dated.title: Dated, not remembered
dated.body: Each entry is recorded on the day it happens.

consistent.title: Consistent over time
consistent.body: The same symptom categories and severity scale every time, so change is visible.

descriptive.title: Descriptive, not diagnostic
descriptive.body: EMBR describes what you logged. It does not tell you what is causing it.

privacy.headline: Your record belongs to you.
privacy.body: EMBR is built so that your health record stays under your control.

yours.title: Built from your entries
yours.body: Every pattern and summary is computed from what you've logged, not blended with anyone else's data.

export.title: Take it with you
export.body: Export your symptom logs, cycle entries and treatments as CSV, or a clinician summary as PDF, whenever you choose.

delete.title: Delete your account
delete.body: Deleting your account removes your symptom logs, cycle entries, daily context, treatments, briefs and settings from EMBR.

sessions.title: See where you're signed in
sessions.body: Review your active sessions and sign out of any device from Settings.

employer.title: If your employer offers EMBR
employer.body: Organization admins see only aggregated, anonymized trends, and nothing at all when a group is too small to keep individuals from being identified. They never see your individual symptom logs or briefs.

cta.headline: Your symptoms are data. Let's make them useful.

footer.disclaimer: EMBR is not a diagnostic tool and does not provide medical advice. Talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your health.

SafetyNotice.heading: When to seek urgent help
SafetyNotice.body: EMBR is a place to keep a record. It cannot tell whether something is an emergency. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, very heavy bleeding, or a sudden severe symptom, call your local emergency number now (for example 112 in the EU, 999 in the UK, 119 in Japan).
SafetyNotice.selfHarm: If you are thinking about harming yourself, contact emergency services or a crisis line in your area right away.

SymptomHistory.noHistoryBody: There are no entries for this symptom yet. Once you log it, its history will appear here.
SymptomHistory.highestSeverityNote: Each logged day shows the highest severity recorded that day.
SymptomHistory.loadError: Your symptom history could not be loaded. Please try again.

CheckIn.title: How are you feeling today?
CheckIn.intro: Select any symptoms you have today, then choose how severe each one is. Anything you don't select is simply not recorded today.
CheckIn.severityRequired: Choose Mild, Moderate or Severe for each selected symptom.
CheckIn.saved: Today's check in is saved. You can edit it until the end of today.
CheckIn.savedEmpty: Today's check in now has no symptoms recorded.
CheckIn.saveError: Your check in could not be saved. Please try again.
CheckIn.loadError: Today's check in could not be loaded. Please try again.
CheckIn.severityGuide: Mild: noticeable. Moderate: gets in the way of your day. Severe: hard to get through your day.
